title: A pull CDN: one user pays, everyone after them doesn't
description: The first request for an object in a region misses and is fetched from origin. Every subsequent request in that region is served from the edge, 20 ms away instead of 200.

nodes.label: What kills hit rate
nodes.sublabel:
Cache-busting query strings,
Vary on a high-cardinality header,
Set-Cookie on static assets,
and needlessly short TTLs.

flows.name: Cold: the first request in a region

steps.text: User A requests an asset. DNS pointed them at the nearest edge, so this hop is short.
The edge has never seen this object, so it fetches from origin — the full long-distance round trip. User A pays it, and the edge stores the response with its TTL.
User A gets the object. Their experience is no better than having no CDN, which is the honest cost of a pull CDN's first request.
User B requests the same object and it is served straight from the edge, roughly 20 ms away.

This is the path that is now NOT taken — origin sees nothing at all. Because popularity follows a steep power law, the overwhelming majority of requests skip this hop, and that ratio is exactly what hit rate measures. A hit-rate regression almost always means someone changed a header, not that traffic changed.
For a scheduled release, thousands of edges are all cold simultaneously. Every one of them misses at once and stampedes your origin — the CDN delivers the exact load it was meant to absorb.
Pushing content to the edges before launch converts that spike into ordinary warm traffic. The same reasoning as cache warm-up, one layer out.
